_note: ThusoIQ — the clinical workflow kernel, as data. Five engines carry a visit from the appointment to the medicine handed over: appointments, consultations, diagnosis, dispensary and wearables. The engines live in packages/thusoiq and hold no sentence of their own; every word a person reads when the kernel says no is one of the refusals below, resolved by id. Read by the web app through packages/thusoiq/contract.ts and generated into Swift and Kotlin by scripts/emit-thusoiq.mjs. Nothing here is a real service: no visit is booked, no medicine is dispensed, no device is read and no clinical decision is issued. The roles come from packages/catalog/vetting.json, the record types and the four SOAP headings from packages/catalog/records.json, and the honesty of each capability from packages/catalog/capabilities.json — so a lapsed registration stops a consultation on this screen by the same arithmetic that withdraws a dispatch on the board.
_whyTheSentencesLiveHere: The kernel shipped with its refusals as string literals in TypeScript. It worked, and it was wrong: iOS and Android could only refuse the same thing in their own words, and a patient told two different stories about why their medicine was held is a patient who believes neither. The sentence is now the contract and the code is the arithmetic that reaches for it. Each refusal carries a `why` as well as a `sentence`, because the sentence is written for the person being refused and the reasoning is written for whoever is about to delete it at eleven at night with a failing test in front of them.
_lawNote: Three separate laws meet inside this kernel and none of them is restated here, only designed around. A diagnosis is an act reserved to a registered practitioner, which is why a nurse may propose an assessment and only a doctor may confirm one or sign the encounter. Dispensing is a licensed activity under the Medicines and Related Substances Act 101 of 1965, which is why the request, the verification and the release are three acts by two different registered people and never one button. Everything the engines touch is health information, and therefore special personal information under section 26 of the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 — which is why consent is checked before a consultation opens rather than at the point of sharing, and why withdrawing wearable consent deletes the samples already received instead of merely closing the tap. No wording here has been read by a lawyer, a nurse, a doctor or a pharmacist.
capabilitiesNote: Named rather than invented. Every one of these is simulated or absent in packages/catalog/capabilities.json, and this kernel is the simulation — a sandbox in memory, seeded with three fictional patients, holding nothing when the tab closes.
recordTypesNote: The record types in packages/catalog/records.json that this kernel writes to. It is a list of ids and not a list of definitions: what each one is, which area it belongs to and who may open it are that file's, and the generator fails if a name here is not one of them.

clinicalRoles.may: Schedule and move a visit, open and write a consultation, propose an assessment, record a wearable connection.
clinicalRoles.mayNot: Confirm an assessment, sign an encounter, request a medicine or dispense one.
clinicalRoles.why: A nurse records what was found. A diagnosis is a reserved act, and a form that lets a nurse write one has not made her a prescriber — it has made the record wrong and left her carrying it.

clinicalRoles.may: Everything a nurse may, and confirming an assessment, signing an encounter and requesting a medicine.
clinicalRoles.why: The person who prescribes is not the person who checks the prescription. That separation is the whole of medicine safety and it survives here even though both are fictional.

clinicalRoles.may: Verify a request against the original and the allergy record, hold it with a written reason, release it against a named batch.
clinicalRoles.mayNot: Write a consultation, propose or confirm an assessment, or request a medicine.
clinicalRoles.why: It names the pharmacy role in vetting.json rather than a role of its own, because what is vetted in South Africa is the premises and its responsible pharmacist. A registration that lapses there stops a release here.

clinicalRolesNote: Three roles, and the honest statement of each is what it may NOT do. Verification itself is not modelled here: `verified` arrives from the host, and packages/catalog/vetting.json owns what being verified means and which checks decide it.

soap.derive: the name of each section, lowercased
soap.why: The four headings are not written down here. They are records.json's, they already appear on the consultation form in all three apps, and a second list would be the copy that drifts. `mustBe` is 4 because two of the refusals below say the word ‘four’ out loud, so the day somebody adds a fifth section the generator fails rather than the sentence quietly becoming a lie.

states.name: Scheduled
states.detail: A time and a clinician are held. Nobody has arrived.

states.name: Arrived
states.detail: The visit has started. A consultation may now be opened against it.

states.name: Completed
states.detail: The encounter is signed and the visit is closed.

states.name: Cancelled
states.detail: Called off, with a reason on the record.

appointments.transitionsNote: The table was a Record literal in appointments.ts and is now the only copy. Two things it refuses on purpose: an appointment cannot go back to scheduled once somebody has arrived, and neither terminal state has a way out. A visit that can be un-completed is a record that can be rewritten after it was signed, and a cancellation that can be reversed is a cancellation reason nobody has to mean.

modes.name: At home
modes.detail: A nurse travels to the address on the visit.

modes.name: By video
modes.detail: A teleconsultation. packages/catalog/teleconsult.json owns what may and may not be done in one.

appointments.modesNote: Two, and the refusal sentence for a missing mode names both by id. The generator checks that it still does, so a third mode cannot be added without somebody reading the sentence a patient sees.

metrics.name: Heart rate
metrics.why: A number a device produced, shown beside the time it was measured and never on its own. It is evidence a clinician may look at, not a finding.

metrics.name: Steps
metrics.why: A count. It is here because a device sends it, and it is deliberately not a target, a goal or a trend — see packages/catalog/wellbeing.json, which refuses all three.

wearables.unitsNote: The map was a ternary chain in wearables.ts. A sample whose unit does not match its metric is rejected rather than converted, because a kernel that quietly converts a unit is a kernel that will one day quietly convert the wrong one.

qualities.name: Accepted
qualities.detail: The device reported a clean reading.

qualities.name: Poor contact
qualities.detail: The device reported it was not sitting properly. Stored, and never treated as the latest value.

wearables.sourcesNote: One source, and it is labelled a simulator. There is no device in this product: `devices` is a simulated capability, and a sample that did not say where it came from could be mistaken for one that did.
wearables.neverInferred: No engine reads a sample and concludes anything. A heart rate does not raise an assessment, does not escalate a visit and does not appear in a diagnosis unless a clinician typed it there as evidence under their own name.

appointmentMinutes.why: Ten minutes is the shortest thing that is still a visit rather than a diary artefact; three hours is the longest before a clinician's whole day has been given to one address and the board stops being true.

noteCharacters.why: Long enough that nobody truncates a history to fit. The cap exists because an unbounded text field on a clinical record is a place a whole scanned document ends up pasted, and then travels wherever the record travels.

quantity.why: A whole number, because half a dispensed unit is a typing error somebody is about to swallow, and a ceiling because a quantity with an extra digit on it is the most ordinary medication error there is.

futureToleranceMs.why: A minute of slack for a device whose clock runs fast. Anything measured further ahead than that was not measured — and a reading dated tomorrow sorts above a real one taken this morning.

idempotencyKeyCharacters.why: The key is the caller's, so it is bounded here. Retries are the normal condition of a phone on a taxi rank, and a command that commits twice because the key was rejected is a medicine dispensed twice.

sampleStaleAfterMs.why: Five minutes, after which the latest reading is labelled stale rather than shown as current. A number with no time attached is the oldest way to mislead a clinician who is in a hurry.

sampleBuffer.why: The sandbox holds a fixed window and forgets the rest. It is a preview, and a preview that accumulates a person's heart rate without bound has started keeping health data.

auditBuffer.why: Who did what, in order, bounded the same way. A real deployment appends this forever and never in memory; the shape is here so the screens are honest about it existing.

boundsNote: Every number the kernel enforces, in one place, each with the reason it is that number and not another. Two of the refusal sentences are filled from these values rather than repeating them, so a bound cannot be changed without the sentence changing with it.
fieldLabelsNote: A label is half of a refusal here — ‘Hold reason is required’ is the sentence somebody reads — so the labels are contract too, and are filled into the text-required refusal rather than concatenated on three platforms.

refusals.sentence: Professional verification is required.
refusals.why: The first gate and the widest one: nothing at all happens for an unverified actor, not even reading. It sits above the role check so that a lapsed doctor is stopped before the kernel has to reason about what doctors may do.

refusals.sentence: A verified professional with the required role must perform this action.
refusals.why: The sentence names the role requirement without naming the role, because telling somebody which registration would have let them through is telling them what to claim next time.

refusals.sentence: Care consent is required before continuing.
refusals.why: Checked before a consultation opens rather than at the point of sharing. Health information is special personal information under POPIA section 26, and consent obtained after the record exists is consent to something already done.

refusals.sentence: Patient not found in this care workspace.
refusals.why: Deliberately the same answer whether the patient does not exist or merely is not this clinician's. A distinction here would turn the kernel into a way of confirming that a named person is a MyThuso patient.

refusals.sentence: This item does not belong to the selected patient.
refusals.why: Every record is fetched by its id AND the patient's. Substituting one id for another is the cheapest way to read somebody else's record, and it must fail as a not-found rather than as a permission message that confirms the record exists.

refusals.sentence: {label} is required (maximum {max} characters).
refusals.why: One sentence for every required free-text field, filled with the field's own label, so that nine fields cannot drift into nine ways of asking for the same thing. The maximum is filled from bounds.noteCharacters rather than written into the sentence.

refusals.sentence: An idempotency key is required.
refusals.why: A command with no key cannot be recognised as a retry. On a phone that drops its connection halfway through a request, that is how one medicine request becomes two.

refusals.sentence: This idempotency key was used for a different command.
refusals.why: A replay returns what the first attempt returned. A key reused for a different command is not a retry, it is a collision, and answering it with the earlier result would tell a caller that something happened which did not.

refusals.sentence: The workspace changed. Refresh before trying again.
refusals.why: Two clinicians on one patient is the normal case, not the edge case. The loser of the race is told to look again, because the alternative is writing over a colleague's note without either of them knowing.

refusals.sentence: Unknown engine command.
refusals.why: The last line of execute(). A command that matches no engine is refused rather than ignored, so a typo in a command name cannot look like success.

refusals.sentence: That appointment status change is not allowed.
refusals.why: The table in appointments.transitions is the whole answer. Said without naming the allowed destinations, because the screen already shows what a person may do and a refusal that lists the alternatives reads as an invitation to try them.

refusals.sentence: The consultation must be signed before completing this appointment.
refusals.why: Completing a visit is the operational act; signing is the clinical one. Allowing the first without the second produces a closed visit with nobody's name on what was decided in it — which is exactly the record that is looked for when something went wrong.

refusals.sentence: Only a scheduled appointment can be moved.
refusals.why: Once a clinician has arrived, the time on the record is a fact about what happened rather than a plan. Moving it afterwards edits history.

refusals.sentence: Choose a future appointment time.
refusals.why: A visit booked into the past is either a typing error or a record being backdated, and the kernel cannot tell which. Both are refused at the door.

refusals.sentence: Duration must be between {min} and {max} minutes.
refusals.why: Filled from bounds.appointmentMinutes, because the two numbers in this sentence are the same two numbers the check uses and a person reading it is about to type one of them.

refusals.sentence: Choose home or video.
refusals.why: Names both modes by id, and the generator fails if a mode is added that the sentence does not name — so the third one cannot be introduced without somebody reading what the patient is asked.

refusals.sentence: This patient or clinician already has an overlapping appointment.
refusals.why: Both directions are checked and the sentence says both. A double-booked clinician is a late visit; a double-booked patient is two clinicians arriving at one house, which is the same person's medicine being discussed twice by people who cannot see each other.

refusals.sentence: Check the patient in before opening a consultation.
refusals.why: The consultation hangs off an appointment somebody has arrived at. Opening one before arrival produces an encounter record for a visit that had not started.

refusals.sentence: This appointment already has a consultation.
refusals.why: One encounter per visit. A second one is how the same visit ends up with two sets of notes, one of them signed and the other the one somebody reads.

refusals.sentence: Signed consultations are immutable. Start a new encounter for further care.
refusals.why: A signature is a statement about what was written at the moment it was signed. Editing afterwards makes the signature a statement about something else, and the second sentence exists so the refusal also says what to do instead.

refusals.sentence: Each note must be text of at most {max} characters.
refusals.why: The per-section cap, filled from bounds.noteCharacters. Separate from text-required because saving a draft does not require every section to be filled — only that none of them is unbounded.

refusals.sentence: Complete all four SOAP sections before requesting review.
refusals.why: A doctor asked to review a half-written note either sends it back or, worse, reviews it. The word ‘four’ is held to records.json's soap list by the generator.

refusals.sentence: Complete all four SOAP sections before signing.
refusals.why: Checked again at signing rather than trusted from the submission, because the note can be edited between the two and the signature is what the record carries afterwards.

refusals.sentence: Review and confirm the clinical assessment before signing.
refusals.why: The signature is what makes the encounter clinical, so what is being signed must already have been decided by somebody entitled to decide it. A signed encounter with an unreviewed assessment inside it is a diagnosis nobody made.

refusals.sentence: This encounter is already signed.
refusals.why: Proposing an assessment against a signed encounter would attach a new clinical opinion to a closed record under somebody else's signature.

refusals.sentence: Review the existing assessment before creating another.
refusals.why: One open assessment at a time. Two competing impressions on one encounter is a doctor choosing which to review, and the one not chosen stays on the record unanswered.

refusals.sentence: This assessment has already been reviewed.
refusals.why: A review is a decision with a name and a rationale on it. Reviewing it again would overwrite whose decision it was.

refusals.sentence: Choose a review decision.
refusals.why: Confirmed or rejected, and nothing in between. There is no ‘noted’ here: a doctor who has looked at an assessment has either accepted it into the record or has not.

refusals.sentence: A signed consultation is required before requesting medicine.
refusals.why: A prescription is a conclusion. Requesting one against an unsigned encounter would let the medicine exist before the reasoning that justifies it does.

refusals.sentence: Quantity must be a whole number between {min} and {max}.
refusals.why: Filled from bounds.quantity. The word ‘whole’ is in the sentence because the most common way this field is got wrong is a decimal point, not a number that is too large.

refusals.sentence: This request has already been dispensed.
refusals.why: The stock movement and the status change commit together, so a second release cannot take a second lot of stock off the shelf. The refusal is what the person holding the packet reads.

refusals.sentence: Verify the original prescription and reconcile the allergy record first.
refusals.why: Three things at once: the original was seen, the allergies were checked, and the allergy record on the patient is actually reconciled rather than merely ticked on this screen. A tick a pharmacist can supply without the record agreeing is a tick that means nothing.

refusals.sentence: Choose a matching, unexpired stock batch.
refusals.why: The batch must be the same item and still in date. A batch chosen by id alone is how a pharmacy dispenses the right name out of the wrong box.

refusals.sentence: There is not enough stock in this batch.
refusals.why: A short batch is refused rather than split across two, because a part-supply that nobody recorded as a part-supply is a patient who runs out early and does not know it.

refusals.sentence: Verify the prescription and recipient before release.
refusals.why: The last check before the medicine leaves the counter, and the only one about who is standing there. The right medicine handed to the wrong person is a dispensing error however correct the box is.

refusals.sentence: Stock is insufficient or expired. Verify a new batch.
refusals.why: Checked again at release rather than trusted from the verification, because time passes between the two and a batch can expire in it. The second sentence says what to do rather than leaving somebody to work it out at a counter.

refusals.sentence: No wearable connection exists for this patient.
refusals.why: A connection record has to be created deliberately before anything about a device can be set. There is no path here that brings a patient's device into existence as a side effect of a sample arriving.

refusals.sentence: Connection and consent must be explicit.
refusals.why: Both are booleans and neither has a default. A consent that arrives as undefined and is read as false is luck; a consent that arrives as undefined and is read as true is the thing this refusal exists to make impossible.

refusals.sentence: Explicit wearable sharing consent is required.
refusals.why: Care consent is not device consent. Agreeing to be treated at home is not agreeing to a continuous stream of your heart rate, and POPIA treats the second as its own purpose.

refusals.sentence: Wearable sharing is paused or consent has been withdrawn.
refusals.why: One sentence for both, because a device that could tell them apart could tell whether a withdrawal had happened. Withdrawal also deletes the samples already received: a tap that is merely closed leaves the water in the bucket.

refusals.sentence: The sample belongs to a different patient.
refusals.why: The patient on the sample and the patient on the command must agree. A device swapped between two people in one household is the ordinary case, not the attack.

refusals.sentence: The sandbox accepts labelled simulator samples only.
refusals.why: Nothing here is a real device, and the kernel refuses to accept anything claiming to be one. The day a real device is connected, this refusal is the thing that has to be deliberately changed.

refusals.sentence: Sample and device identifiers are required.
refusals.why: Without both, a duplicate cannot be recognised and a reading cannot be traced back to the thing that produced it.

refusals.sentence: Sample type, unit or numeric value is invalid.
refusals.why: One sentence for the metric, its unit and its number, because they are one decision: a value is only meaningful in the unit its metric is measured in. Rejected rather than converted — see wearables.unitsNote.

refusals.sentence: Sample quality is required.
refusals.why: A device that knows its contact was poor must say so. A reading with no quality on it would be indistinguishable from a good one and would become the latest value on a clinician's screen.

refusals.sentence: Sample time is invalid or in the future.
refusals.why: Measurement time is what orders the readings, not arrival time. A sample dated tomorrow would sit permanently above every real one, so it is refused past bounds.futureToleranceMs.

refusals.sentence: Duplicate sample already received.
refusals.why: A device that retries is a device working correctly. Storing the retry would put the same heartbeat on the record twice and make a resend look like a trend.

neverInThisKernel: No engine here interprets a clinical value, scores a patient, ranks a queue, suggests a diagnosis, or lets one person perform two of the three dispensing acts. There is no override, no force flag and no administrative path that skips a check — an operator who needs one of these refusals lifted needs a clinician, not a button.
